Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (RIN 0938-AV44)

Dear Administrator Oz:
AstraZeneca appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization Proposed Rule (the Proposed Rule) published by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) on April 14, 2026. AstraZeneca is a global, science-led biopharmaceutical company focused on the discovery, development, and commercialization of prescription medicines, primarily in the areas of Oncology; Cardiovascular, Renal, and Metabolism (CVRM); and Respiratory and Immunology. Through our subsidiary Alexion, AstraZeneca is also dedicated to addressing the needs of patients living with rare diseases.
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** AstraZeneca (signed by Sarah C. Arbes, Head of US Federal Affairs and Policy)
- **Stakeholder type:** Other (global biopharmaceutical manufacturer; operates through subsidiary Alexion for rare diseases; participates in all major U.S. payer markets)
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Global biopharmaceutical company operating in 100+ countries; 18,000+ U.S. employees; supports ~92,000 U.S. jobs; specialty in oncology, CVRM, respiratory/immunology, and rare diseases via Alexion; extensive payer and formulary engagement experience

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

AstraZeneca broadly supports the proposed rule as a critical and long-overdue step toward closing the regulatory gap between medical services and prescription drugs in prior authorization. The company provides highly detailed recommendations across nearly every major provision, including: supporting the October 1, 2027 implementation date; recommending a uniform 24-hour PA decision standard across all payer markets; urging strong transparency and AI guardrails for denial rationales; advocating for plan-level and point-of-sale reporting; and calling for robust safeguards for rare disease patients who face disproportionate harm from PA delays and step therapy requirements. AstraZeneca also recommends additional reforms not directly covered by the proposed rule, including prohibitions on retroactive denials, white-bagging/brown-bagging mandates, and inadequate single case agreement processes.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, API-USAGE-METRICS, PA-DENIAL-REASONS, PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS, API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING, GENERAL (step therapy RFI, other reforms)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (April 14, 2026); 85 Fed. Reg. 25510 (2020 Interop Rule); 89 Fed. Reg. 8758 (2024 PA Final Rule); 42 C.F.R. § 423.568; 42 C.F.R. § 438.404(b)(2); Social Security Act § 1927(k)(2)(B) and (k)(3); 45 CFR 156.223(h); 90 FR 15792 (April 2025 MA Final Rule); 89 Fed. Reg. 51,238
- **Standards referenced:** NCPDP SCRIPT standard, NCPDP Formulary and Benefit (F&B) standard, NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standard, HL7 FHIR, Prior Authorization API (CRD/DTR/PAS IGs), Patient Access API, Provider Access API, Payer-to-Payer API

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: PA-DRUG-PHARMACY — NCPDP Standards**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support with enhancements
- **Rationale:** Broad adoption of NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB standards will improve transparency, reduce administrative inefficiency, and facilitate timely prescribing decisions. Critical for rare disease patients who face complex PA requirements and community pharmacy unfamiliarity.
- **Specific request:** (1) Require weekly F&B data updates to ensure accuracy; (2) clarify that all claim-level restrictions resulting in rejected or modified claims (including POS claim edits) are treated as PA transactions subject to NCPDP standards and disclosure.

**Topic 2: PA-DRUG-MEDICAL — Prior Authorization API**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support with enhancements
- **Rationale:** PA API will reduce administrative burden, improve turnaround times, and is especially important for rare disease therapies (infused enzymes, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapies) that currently use manual multi-week processes.
- **Specific request:** Adopt safeguards to prevent PA from being used to steer patients to payer-preferred (often payer-affiliated) sites of care; require site-of-care conditions to be disclosed via PA API and subject to same justification and appeal rights as denials.

**Topic 3: Implementation Timeline and Extension Pathways**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, STATE-EXTENSION-PROCESS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** October 1, 2027 provides a reasonable timeframe; extension pathway for state Medicaid/CHIP FFS is appropriate.
- **Specific request:** Limit extensions to a defined period (no more than 6 months total); require showing of demonstrable technical/operational barriers; allow QHP issuers on FFEs to request exceptions through annual certification process under 45 CFR 156.223(h).

**Topic 4: Compliance Certification and Delegated Entity Accountability**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Payers could maintain nominal compliance while relying on older standards in live transactions; delegated entities (PBMs, UM vendors) administer core PA functions but may not be subject to same standards.
- **Specific request:** Require compliance certification based on live transaction data (not just system support); require transaction-level auditing; establish dedicated compliance audit mechanism extending to PBMs and UM vendors.

**Topic 5: Concurrent Review**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Concurrent review functions as de facto PA but may not be subject to same transparency/timeliness standards; particularly burdensome for rare disease patients requiring lifelong therapy with frequent reauthorizations.
- **Specific request:** Clarify that concurrent review is subject to same transparency, electronic workflow, and timeliness standards; F&B files should indicate reauthorization requirements.

**Topic 6: Access APIs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL (implicitly), API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with enhancements
- **Rationale:** Making PA request and decision data available through Access APIs reduces duplicative submissions and improves treatment planning; formulary removal from Provider/Payer-to-Payer APIs should be sequenced carefully.
- **Specific request:** (1) Phase formulary removal only after Prior Authorization API is fully operational; (2) include additional data elements: decision-making entity identity, step therapy status, authorization end dates, clinical criteria version applied; (3) require near-real-time updates (within 12 hours of determination); (4) define covered drug scope broadly and explicitly, preventing carve-outs for biosimilars, compounded drugs, vaccines.

**Topic 7: PA Decision Timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify (strengthen)
- **Rationale:** Varying market-specific timeframes create complexity and risk slower routing; 72-hour standard is insufficient for oncology, rare disease, and acute infectious disease patients where delays cause irreversible harm.
- **Specific request:** Adopt uniform 24-hour standard across all impacted payers including MA and Part D; if not, extend 24-hour standard to all Medicaid drug requests and establish default expedited pathways for oncology, rare disease, and acute infectious disease categories; establish 5-business-day outer limit on total PA decision time; require pend only once per request with documented reason; auto-approve pending specialized review if 24-hour limit cannot be met.

**Topic 8: PA Denial Reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with significant enhancements
- **Rationale:** Existing denial communications are vague and insufficient; rare disease specialists cannot effectively appeal without knowing specific clinical criteria applied; AI is increasingly used in PA decisions without disclosure or qualified review.
- **Specific request:** (1) Require denial rationales to be sent directly to both providers AND patients; (2) require: specific criterion not met, evidence standard/guideline applied, documentation needed to obtain approval; (3) prohibit withholding criteria based on proprietary claims; (4) develop standardized denial categories with patient advocate and specialist input; (5) require disclosure of AI use in denial communications; (6) require AI-influenced denials to be reviewed by clinician with relevant specialty training; (7) apply rationale requirements to all denial types including administrative/technical denials.

**Topic 9: API Usage Metrics (Payer Reporting to CMS)**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with enhancements
- **Rationale:** Contract/issuer-level aggregation masks variation and outlier behavior; metrics should reflect actual patient access impact, not just API utilization counts.
- **Specific request:** (1) Require plan-level reporting; (2) add access/performance measures: denial rates stratified by therapeutic area and drug type, appeal overturn rates, time-to-decision by drug class, step therapy failure rates; (3) CMS should aggregate and publish annual report; (4) define reportable PA transactions broadly to include claims edits, concurrent review, re-authorization, and formulary exceptions.

**Topic 10: Public Reporting of Rx PA Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING, API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with significant enhancements
- **Rationale:** Public data will promote accountability, but aggregate reporting masks variation, POS rejections are excluded, and Part D is excluded creating a transparency gap.
- **Specific request:** (1) Plan-level granularity; (2) stratification by drug type (brand, generic, biosimilar) and therapeutic area, with rare disease separate; (3) include POS claim rejections; (4) extend to Medicare Part D; (5) require annual CMS analysis and public publication; (6) require sub-reporting for delegated entities; (7) report authorization duration by drug class; (8) distinguish conditional approvals from clean approvals; (9) require public disclosure of UM policies and clinical criteria in machine-readable format, prohibiting withholding on proprietary grounds.

**Topic 11: Step Therapy (RFI)**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support with comprehensive reform framework
- **Rationale:** Step therapy is particularly harmful for rare disease patients who often have a single FDA-approved treatment; plan-year resets force patients to retry failed therapies; current opacity prevents oversight.
- **Specific request:** (1) Require transparent disclosure of step therapy protocols; (2) honor step therapy outcomes across plan transitions; (3) automatic exceptions when prescriber attests contraindication, prior failure, or clinical inappropriateness; (4) explicitly prohibit step therapy when no therapeutic alternative exists; (5) prohibit plan-year resets for documented failures; (6) prohibit mid-year imposition on stable patients; (7) establish federal definition of "previously failed" therapy including adverse effects, contraindications, and prescriber determination of inappropriateness; use collected data to develop evidence-based guardrails.

**Topic 12: Other Prior Authorization Reforms**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Recommend additional actions
- **Rationale:** Single case agreements, retroactive denials, administrative denials without outreach, peer-to-peer delays, copay tier exceptions, and white/brown-bagging all function as access barriers without equivalent regulatory safeguards.
- **Specific request:** (1) Develop guardrails for single case agreements including transparency of coverage criteria and timely response requirements; (2) prohibit retroactive denials after valid PA and dispensing (permit only for documented fraud); (3) require good-faith provider outreach before administrative denial; (4) require peer-to-peer review offered within 24 hours and completed within applicable timeline; (5) apply PA requirements to copay tier exception process; (6) prohibit white-bagging and brown-bagging mandates requiring use of PBM-affiliated specialty pharmacies.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S14:** Supports non-Part D NCPDP applicability; recommends scope include all claim-level restrictions and POS edits, not just formal PA.
- **S22:** Does not raise cost concerns; instead supports NCPDP adoption and recommends weekly F&B data updates.
- **S25:** Notes RTPB maturity is adequate; supports adoption with caveat that all claim-level restrictions be captured.
- **S12:** Highlights technical implementation considerations for medical benefit PA API; recommends site-of-care safeguards and concurrent review clarity.
- **S16:** Recommends standardized denial categories; requires: criterion not met, evidence standard, documentation needed; prohibits withholding criteria on proprietary grounds.
- **S17:** Urges CMS to develop standardized denial codes with input from patient advocates and specialty physicians; also require AI disclosure.
- **S20:** Recommends uniform 24-hour standard across all programs; recommends 5-business-day outer limit; requests default expedited pathways for high-risk therapeutic categories.
- **S21:** Supports October 1, 2027; recommends extension limits (max 6 months) and live-transaction compliance certification.
- **S29:** Recommends broader definition of reportable PA transactions; plan-level reporting; stratification by therapeutic area.
- **S30:** Recommends POS rejections be included in public metrics; addresses broad coverage of all access-limiting mechanisms.
- **S34:** Recommends annual CMS publication of aggregated analysis of reported metrics.
- **S35:** Supports public aggregate reporting; recommends rare disease stratification and sub-reporting for delegated entities.
- **S38/S39:** Recommends limiting extension duration to 6 months maximum with demonstrable-barrier showing.
- **S31:** Recommends QHP exception process through annual certification; supports extension pathway concept.
- **S66 (Step Therapy RFI):** Comprehensive step therapy reform framework including plan-year reset prohibition, "previously failed" definition, and rare disease exemption.

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require weekly updates to NCPDP F&B data files to ensure accuracy at point of prescribing.
2. Clarify that all claim-level restrictions resulting in rejected/modified pharmacy claims (including POS edits) are treated as PA transactions subject to NCPDP standards.
3. Require site-of-care conditions in PA approvals to be disclosed via PA API and subject to same justification/appeal standards as denials.
4. Limit state Medicaid/CHIP FFS extension periods to no more than 6 months total; require demonstrable barrier showing.
5. Allow QHP issuers to request exceptions through annual FFE certification process.
6. Require compliance certification based on live transaction data with transaction-level auditing.
7. Establish dedicated compliance audit mechanism extending to PBMs and UM vendors.
8. Clarify concurrent review requirements are subject to same transparency, electronic workflow, and timeliness standards as prospective PA.
9. Phase formulary data removal from Provider/Payer-to-Payer APIs only after PA API is fully operational.
10. Add data elements to Access APIs: decision-making entity identity, step therapy status, authorization end dates, clinical criteria version.
11. Require near-real-time Access API updates (within 12 hours of determination); subject to audit for accuracy.
12. Define covered drug scope for Access APIs broadly and explicitly to prevent carve-outs.
13. Adopt uniform 24-hour PA decision standard across all impacted payers and programs.
14. If uniform standard not adopted, extend 24-hour standard to all Medicaid drugs and establish default expedited pathways for oncology, rare disease, and acute infectious disease categories.
15. Establish 5-business-day outer limit on total PA decision time; limit pends to one occurrence with documented reason; auto-approve if qualified review cannot be completed within 24 hours.
16. Require denial rationales to be communicated directly to both providers and patients with next-steps guidance.
17. Require denial rationales to identify: specific criterion not met, evidence standard applied, documentation needed for approval.
18. Prohibit withholding PA criteria on proprietary/confidentiality grounds.
19. Develop standardized denial categories with input from patient advocates and specialty physicians.
20. Require disclosure of AI use in denial communications; require AI-influenced denials to be reviewed by specialty-trained clinician.
21. Apply specific denial rationale requirements to all denial types including administrative/technical denials.
22. Require plan-level API usage reporting rather than contract/issuer level.
23. Add access/performance measures to API metrics: denial rates stratified by therapeutic area/drug type, appeal overturn rates, time-to-decision, step therapy failure rates.
24. Define reportable PA transactions broadly to include claims edits, concurrent review, re-authorization, and formulary exceptions.
25. Include POS claim rejections in publicly reported PA metrics.
26. Extend public reporting requirements to Medicare Part D.
27. Require CMS to publish annual analysis of prior authorization metrics across programs.
28. Require sub-reporting for delegated entities (PBMs, UM vendors) in public metrics.
29. Require public reporting of authorization duration by drug class.
30. Require separate reporting of conditional approvals distinguishing from clean approvals.
31. Require public disclosure of UM policies and clinical criteria in machine-readable format.
32. Require transparent disclosure of step therapy protocols separately from PA criteria.
33. Honor step therapy outcomes across plan transitions (prior failed therapy recognized by new payer).
34. Require automatic step therapy exceptions when prescriber attests contraindication, prior failure, or clinical inappropriateness.
35. Prohibit step therapy when no therapeutic alternative exists (particularly for rare diseases).
36. Prohibit plan-year resets for documented prior therapy failures.
37. Prohibit mid-year imposition of step therapy on stable patients without clinical justification.
38. Establish federal definition of "previously failed" therapy including adverse effects, contraindications, and prescriber determination.
39. Develop guardrails for single case agreements including transparency of criteria and timely response requirements.
40. Prohibit retroactive denial of drugs already dispensed following valid PA (except documented fraud).
41. Require good-faith provider outreach before issuing administrative denials.
42. Require peer-to-peer review to be offered within 24 hours of denial and completed within applicable decision timeframe.
43. Apply PA transparency/electronic requirements to copay tier exception process.
44. Prohibit white-bagging and brown-bagging mandates requiring use of PBM-affiliated specialty pharmacies.

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Vague denial rationales harm rare disease patients; POS claim edits function as PA but lack transparency; payers may achieve nominal compliance while using non-compliant standards in live transactions; delegated entity (PBM/UM vendor) noncompliance undermines payer-level requirements; site-of-care steering through PA conditions is used for financial rather than clinical purposes; white/brown-bagging disrupts care quality; single case agreements lack PA safeguards.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** 90%+ of physicians report PA delays negatively impact outcomes; nearly 1 in 4 physicians report PA led to serious adverse event; 75%+ of abandoning patients never initiate alternative therapy within 90 days; practices spend ~$68,000/physician/year on health plan interactions; 39 PA requests per physician per week (~13 hours); aHUS patients face irreversible kidney damage within 48-72 hours; PNH patients face life-threatening thrombosis during review periods; complement-mediated disease patients require lifelong therapy with frequent reauthorization burden.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Delegated entity (PBM/UM vendor) compliance gaps; live-transaction vs. nominal compliance gap; concurrent review not clearly covered; Access API data currency insufficient for time-sensitive therapies; point-of-sale edits excluded from current PA framework.

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** 90%+ of physicians report PA delays negatively impact patient outcomes (AMA 2024 and 2026 surveys); nearly 1 in 4 physicians report PA led to serious adverse event (AMA May 2026 survey); 75%+ patients who abandon prescription fail to initiate alternative within 90 days; practices spend ~$68,000/physician/year on health plan interactions; 39 PA requests/physician/week (~13 hours); 40% of physicians hired staff exclusively for PA; 88%+ report PA contributes to burnout; 75% of dermatology PA denial letters did not identify decision maker.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA 2024 Prior Authorization Physician Survey; AMA May 2026 Prior Authorization Physician Survey; NORD 2023 barriers report; Loirat & Frémeaux-Bacchi 2011 (aHUS); Legendre et al. 2013 NEJM (eculizumab in aHUS); Ismail et al. 2023 J. Managed Care & Specialty Pharmacy (cost-sharing and PA effects); Parker et al. 2005 Blood (PNH); Barbieri & Bader 2025 (dermatology denial transparency); multiple AMA Council on Medical Service reports.
- **Examples provided:** aHUS — irreversible kidney damage within 48-72 hours; PNH — life-threatening thrombosis during 72-hour review; complement-mediated disease patients requiring lifelong therapy face annual reauthorization; psychiatric medications — PA leads to higher hospitalization and incarceration rates; buprenorphine-naloxone PA removal increases use; novel anticoagulants PA restriction increases stroke risk.

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Rare disease patients (disproportionate impact), oncology patients, providers (administrative burden reduction), PBMs (compliance extension), UM vendors, pharmacies (retroactive denial risk), payers (compliance certification), CMS (oversight improvement)
- **Economic implications:** PA delays estimated at $68,000/physician/year administrative cost; PA reforms could reduce abandonment rates and downstream hospitalization costs; white/brown-bagging mandates raise patient cost-sharing and reduce care quality; plan-level reporting required to identify outlier payer behavior
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports October 1, 2027 date as reasonable; recommends sequenced formulary API removal to avoid information gaps; near-real-time API updates technically achievable but requires audit mechanisms; POS claim edits already exist and need only definitional clarification to be included
- **Patient care impact:** Very high — PA delays cause irreversible harm in rare disease, oncology, and acute conditions; denial opacity prevents effective appeals; step therapy forces repeated treatment failures and plan-year resets; retroactive denials disrupt established therapy; white/brown-bagging compromises drug integrity

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive (with extensive specific enhancements)
- **Tone:** Technical, Professional, Advocacy-oriented
- **Priority level:** High

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "For patients with rare diseases, prior authorization delays can be particularly devastating. Many rare diseases are progressive, meaning that delays of even days or weeks can result in irreversible organ damage, permanent disability, or death." - Context: Establishing the clinical urgency of PA reform for rare disease patients, particularly those with AstraZeneca/Alexion products.
2. "Absent clear guidance, these claim-level restrictions may fall outside the scope of prior authorization requirements, despite having the same functional impact on patient access. This creates a risk that utilization management controls could be shifted into the claims adjudication process, where they are less visible and not subject to the same safeguards." - Context: Recommending POS claim edits be treated as PA transactions.
3. "It is not sufficient for payers to provide boilerplate explanations that fail to communicate the reason behind the denial." - Context: Advocating for specific, actionable denial rationales.
4. "Without greater visibility into authorization length, approval rates alone may present an incomplete or misleading picture of access. In particular, short-duration authorizations may increase the volume of repeat requests while maintaining superficially favorable approval rates." - Context: Requesting public reporting of authorization duration to reveal access barriers masked by approval rate statistics.

---

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports October 1, 2027; recommends limiting extensions to 6 months; urges live-transaction compliance certification to prevent de facto delays.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Cites $68,000/physician/year administrative cost of PA; notes PA leads to higher overall healthcare utilization and waste.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - 39 PA requests/physician/week; 40% hired dedicated PA staff; 88%+ report PA contributes to burnout; peer-to-peer delays as additional burden.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not directly addressed.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Rare disease patients face disproportionate barriers; geographic inequity in access; step therapy nonsensical for single-FDA-approved-drug conditions.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Recommends sequenced formulary API removal; near-real-time Access API updates; live-transaction compliance testing; POS edits definitional clarification.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Supports both NCPDP and FHIR standards as adequate; focuses more on compliance scope and data quality than IG maturity.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central theme throughout: aHUS, PNH, rare disease patients face life-threatening consequences from PA delays; treatment abandonment rate very high.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Extensive recommendations: denial categories, AI disclosure, UM policy machine-readable files, authorization duration reporting, conditional approval reporting, POS rejection inclusion.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Recommends delegated entity (PBM/UM vendor) accountability mechanisms; coordinated step therapy recognition across plan transitions.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Addresses both pathways in detail; recommends concurrent review and POS edits be subject to same standards regardless of benefit.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - POS claim edits, concurrent review, single case agreements, and white/brown-bagging represent existing practices that circumvent PA safeguards.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - PBMs and UM vendors are core concern: recommends compliance auditing extend to delegated entities; white/brown-bagging by PBM-affiliated specialty pharmacies.
